pages.text:
The Making of the Indian Constitution
History & Civics | Standard 8
1. Why did India need a Constitution?
When India became independent on 15 August 1947, it needed fundamental rules to govern the country. India was a large
and diverse nation, with people belonging to different religions, languages, and communities. A Constitution establishes
how a country is governed, defines the powers of government, protects citizens’ rights, and sets out principles that guide
the nation.
2. The Constituent Assembly
The Constituent Assembly was formed to prepare India’s Constitution. Its members discussed how the country should be
governed and what rights its citizens should enjoy. The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was
elected its permanent President. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft Constitution.
The Assembly debated important questions, including equality, freedom, minority rights, and the structure of government.
These discussions helped shape a Constitution suited to an independent India.
3. Adoption of the Constitution
The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. It came into effect on 26 January 1950, when
India became a republic. Republic Day is celebrated on 26 January each year to commemorate this event.
The Constitution established a democratic system of government. Its Preamble expresses the ideals of justice, liberty,
equality, and fraternity.
Key facts to remember
• 9 December 1946: First meeting of the Constituent Assembly
• Dr. B. R. Ambedkar: Chairman of the Drafting Committee
• 26 November 1949: Constitution adopted
• 26 January 1950: Constitution came into effect; India became a republic
Check your understanding
1. Why did independent India need a Constitution?
2. What was Dr. B. R. Ambedkar’s role in making the Constitution?
3. What is the difference between 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950?
headings: 1. Why did India need a Constitution?
paragraphs: The Making of the Indian Constitution History & Civics | Standard 8

When India became independent on 15 August 1947, it needed fundamental rules to govern the country. India was a large and diverse nation, with people belonging to different religions, languages, and communities. A Constitution establishes how a country is governed, defines the powers of government, protects citizens’ rights, and sets out principles that guide the nation.

The Constituent Assembly was formed to prepare India’s Constitution. Its members discussed how the country should be governed and what rights its citizens should enjoy. The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected its permanent President. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft Constitution. The Assembly debated important questions, including equality, freedom, minority rights, and the structure of government. These discussions helped shape a Constitution suited to an independent India.

The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. It came into effect on 26 January 1950, when India became a republic. Republic Day is celebrated on 26 January each year to commemorate this event. The Constitution established a democratic system of government. Its Preamble expresses the ideals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.
• 9 December 1946: First meeting of the Constituent Assembly
• Dr. B. R. Ambedkar: Chairman of the Drafting Committee
• 26 January 1950: Constitution came into effect; India became a republic

curriculum_relevance.title: Curriculum Relevance
curriculum_relevance.question: Does it test an important, syllabus-central learning point?

scale.1: Tests non-curriculum noise (e.g., publication/reprint dates, ISBNs, page headers) or lacks a learning point.
scale.2: Focuses on a trivial peripheral detail rather than a core concept of the passage.
scale.3: Tests a valid secondary fact or definition from the passage.
scale.4: Tests a primary concept, cause-effect relationship, or scientific/mathematical principle.
scale.5: Directly targets a high-priority learning point central to the ICSE chapter with clear pedagogical purpose.

source_fidelity.title: Source Fidelity
source_fidelity.question: Is the answer directly supported by the supplied material?

scale.1: Unsupported by source, fabricates evidence, invents a page number, or claims to read an unextracted visual diagram/map.
scale.2: Weak token overlap with the supplied source text or relies on unapproved external assumptions.
scale.3: Partially supported by the source passage, with minor paraphrasing drift.
scale.4: Strongly grounded in the supplied text with verifiable evidence overlap and valid page reference.
scale.5: Verbatim or near-verbatim source evidence verified on the exact source page with zero unsupported claims.

clarity.title: Clarity & Specificity
clarity.question: Is the wording specific, unambiguous, and well-structured?

scale.1: Fragmented, ungrammatical, or ambiguous wording that students cannot interpret.
scale.2: Vague prompt (e.g., 'Write about this') lacking a clear task verb or scope.
scale.3: Understandable question with acceptable wording but minor phrasing stiffness.
scale.4: Clear, specific question with an explicit cognitive verb and unambiguous scope.
scale.5: Exemplary, examination-ready ICSE question phrasing with precise terminology and clear task expectations.

educational_value.title: Educational Value
educational_value.question: Does it test meaningful learning rather than mechanical sentence copying?

scale.1: Mechanical fill-in-the-blank or trivial copying of a sentence with zero cognitive demand.
scale.2: Surface-level recall of an isolated word when the passage supports deeper understanding.
scale.3: Tests basic factual recall or definition comprehension appropriately.
scale.4: Requires conceptual explanation, cause-effect reasoning, sequence ordering, or comparison.
scale.5: Engages higher-order application, multi-point synthesis, table interpretation, or quantitative problem solving.

distinctness.title: Distinctness
distinctness.question: Does it add value beyond other questions in the set?

scale.1: Exact or near-exact duplicate of another question or tests the exact same fact in slightly different words.
scale.2: High lexical/conceptual overlap (>= 55% similarity) with an already selected question.
scale.3: Touches a related aspect of the same section with moderate overlap.
scale.4: Tests a distinct concept or applies a different cognitive skill/question type.
scale.5: Completely distinct learning point and question category, maximizing topic coverage.

answer_quality.title: Answer Quality & Notation Accuracy
answer_quality.question: Is the answer accurate, complete, notation-faithful, and deterministically verified?

scale.1: Empty, factually incorrect, fails deterministic math/chemical balance verification, or corrupts scientific notation.
scale.2: Incomplete answer missing key explanation steps or required SI units.
scale.3: Correct core answer but brief or lacking full context.
scale.4: Accurate, complete answer preserving source terminology and notation.
scale.5: Comprehensive, curriculum-grade model answer with verified calculations/balanced equations and exact scientific notation.

grade_suitability.title: ICSE Grade Suitability
grade_suitability.question: Is it appropriate for the specified ICSE class (Classes 8–10 vs Classes 11–12)?

scale.1: Severely mismatched for the target ICSE class (e.g., advanced calculus jargon for Class 8 or trivial one-word recall for Class 12).
scale.2: Vocabulary or expected reasoning depth noticeably above or below the target class band.
scale.3: Acceptable for the class level with minor phrasing adjustments needed.
scale.4: Well-matched to the cognitive and vocabulary expectations of the specified ICSE class.
scale.5: Calibrated specifically to ICSE Class 8–10 (accessible, foundational reasoning) or Class 11–12 (rigorous, analytical/multi-step depth).

all_evaluated_candidates.answer: In chronological order: (1) 9 December 1946 — the Constituent Assembly held its first meeting; (2) 15 August 1947 — India became independent; (3) 26 November 1949 — the Constitution of India was adopted; and (4) 26 January 1950 — the Constitution came into effect, when India became a republic.

all_evaluated_candidates.question: Why did India need a Constitution after becoming independent on 15 August 1947?
all_evaluated_candidates.answer: When India became independent on 15 August 1947, it needed fundamental rules to govern the country. India was a large and diverse nation, with people belonging to different religions, languages, and communities. A Constitution establishes how a country is governed, defines the powers of government, protects citizens’ rights, and sets out principles that guide the nation.

all_evaluated_candidates.question: What is the difference between the significance of 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950 in the making of the Indian Constitution?

all_evaluated_candidates.question: What roles did Dr. Rajendra Prasad and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar play in the Constituent Assembly during the making of the Indian Constitution?
all_evaluated_candidates.answer: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly, while Dr. B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft Constitution.
